correctness.rationale: The proof reduces the problem to the exact packing number of pairwise edge-disjoint edge covers of \(K_s\). The counting upper bound gives at most \(s-1\) covers for even \(s\) and \(s-2\) for odd \(s\); one-factorization attains the even bound, while the explicit near-perfect-matching construction plus distinct Hamilton-path edges attains the odd bound. If two multipartite parts both omit vertices, their cross-edge cannot lie on any selected-endpoint geodesic; hence there is one incomplete part. For each omitted vertex and each full part, its incident edges require one edge cover of that full part, and endpoint-pair uniqueness makes these covers pairwise disjoint. This gives exactly \(r\le R_i\); the converse construction assigns the packed edge covers and covers all remaining cross-edges directly. The enumerator and minimum formulas then follow by counting omissions.
risks: All parts are assumed to have size at least two; singleton parts are excluded.

evidence: The published theorem gives the minimum cardinality; it does not imply which larger subsets are feasible or their counts.

originality.rationale: Klavžar–Zmazek determine the scalar strong edge geodetic number for complete multipartite graphs and prove related necessity/constructions, but their inspected article does not classify every feasible vertex set or give the all-set polynomial/minimum-set count. The audited theorem supplies an iff membership rule using the exact edge-cover packing number, so it is not implied by the published scalar value theorem.

value.rationale: A complete membership theorem and cardinality enumerator for a natural NP-style geodetic covering invariant materially strengthen a published scalar extremal result. The exact edge-cover packing mechanism also explains the parity split in the known value formula and yields all minimum-set counts.
risks: The contribution is restricted to complete multipartite graphs with no singleton parts.

limitations: Complete multipartite graphs with every part at least two only.
Finite verification through order ten is corroboration, not proof.
